learningObjective: Explain the semantics of warps, blocks and grids in CUDA and the resources they share.

canonicalClaims.claim: In CUDA, a warp is 32 threads from a single block scheduled together; a block is assigned to exactly one SM and its threads share shared memory and block-scope barriers; a grid may span many SMs and requires cooperative groups for cross-block synchronization.
conditions: NVIDIA compute capability with warp size 32.
nonImplications: Does not imply all blocks of a grid are resident concurrently.
Does not imply cooperative-groups grid sync is always available (requires cooperative launch and fitting all blocks in GPU).

misconceptions.claim: Warps can be formed across blocks to fill an SM's occupancy.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Warps are formed from consecutive thread indices within a single block; the execution model does not mix blocks into warps.

misconceptions.claim: Shared memory is grid-scope and can be used for cross-block synchronization.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Shared memory is per-SM and per-block; cross-block communication uses global memory + atomics or cooperative groups.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, memory hierarchy

misconceptions.whyWrong: __syncthreads() is a block-scope barrier; grid-level barriers require cooperative groups' grid.sync().
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, cooperative groups

misconceptions.claim: A block may migrate between SMs during execution to balance load.
misconceptions.whyWrong: A block, once assigned to an SM, stays there until it completes; the runtime does not migrate active blocks.

implementationFacts: Block runs on exactly one SM.
__syncthreads() is block-scope; grid.sync() (cooperative groups) is grid-scope.
performanceScenarios: Reductions across the entire grid typically use two-kernel or cooperative-groups schemes because __syncthreads() cannot span blocks.
